fields.title: David Livingstone (For Teens)
fields.description: At ten, David Livingstone was working fourteen-hour days in a Scottish cotton mill, reading a book propped on the spinning machine. He became a doctor and a missionary, was mauled by a lion and saved by an African teacher whose gun misfired, walked across Africa with men who could have abandoned him, and spent his last years among slave traders he could neither stop nor escape. This teen edition tells his story straight: the one known convert, the river that failed, the wife who died beside him, the son he barely knew, and the friends who carried him a thousand miles home.

qa.question: Who was David Livingstone?
qa.answer: A Scottish mill boy, born in 1813 at Blantyre, who became a doctor and went to southern Africa for the London Missionary Society in 1841. He worked among the Batswana, crossed Africa from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean between 1853 and 1856, led a failed government expedition on the Zambezi, and spent his last years searching for the source of the Nile and exposing the East African slave trade. He died at Chitambo’s village, in what is now Zambia, in 1873.

qa.question: Is the book honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It names his one known convert, the river plan that failed at Kebrabasa, his quarrels and unfairness to colleagues, the years his wife Mary spent alone in Britain, her death on the Zambezi, his son Robert’s death in an American prison camp, the slave traders he depended on, and the way his name was later used to justify colonial rule.

qa.question: What did he mean by “I never made a sacrifice”?
qa.answer: In a speech at Cambridge in 1857 he said that serving God in Africa was “emphatically no sacrifice” but a privilege, a small part of a great debt owed to God. The book honours that, and also points out that much of the cost of his calling was paid by others, especially his wife and children.

qa.question: Did Livingstone really make only one convert?
qa.answer: Sechele, chief of the Bakwena, is the only African he is known to have baptised, in 1848, and Livingstone suspended him a few months later. But Sechele kept his faith and led his people in it for the rest of his life, and the missions founded after Livingstone’s death in the lands he explored grew into large African-led churches.

qa.question: How did he treat the African people he lived among?
qa.answer: He learned Setswana by living among the Bakwena, wrote that Africans were in no way inferior to Europeans, and kept his promise to bring twenty-seven men home from Luanda. But he saw little good in African religion and customs, used the prejudiced language of his time, and gave too little credit to the Africans, like Mebalwe, Sechele, Susi and Chuma, who saved and shaped his life.

qa.question: Where do the stories come from?
qa.answer: From the full-length biography of David Livingstone, which draws on his own books and journals, his first biographer’s printing of his letters, and Stanley’s account, checked against modern historians. Uncertain stories, like Stanley’s famous greeting and the exact date of his death, are marked as uncertain. A separate edition for younger children tells the same story more simply.

qa.question: What can a teenager today take from his story?
qa.answer: That God can use a poor, hard-working kid who is bad at public speaking; that keeping your word matters even when it costs you; that your choices have a cost for the people closest to you; and that faithfulness can bear fruit long after you are gone.

qa.question: Who carried his body to the coast?
qa.answer: His African companions, led by Susi and Chuma, with Jacob Wainwright, Matthew Wellington, Carus Farrar, Majwara, Halima, Farijala and many others. They buried his heart under a tree at Chitambo’s village and carried his body about a thousand miles to the coast. Only Jacob Wainwright went to England for the funeral.

fields.title: Six in the Morning
fields.body_html:
“Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in Sheol, whither thou goest.” — Ecclesiastes 9:10 (ASV)

David Livingstone was born on 19 March 1813 at Blantyre Works, a cotton-mill village on the River Clyde, about eight miles from Glasgow in Scotland. The Livingstones lived in Shuttle Row, a tenement built for the workers, and they had one room. In it the parents cooked, ate, slept, read and prayed, and raised their children. David was the second of seven. Two of them died young.

His father, Neil, sold tea from door to door. He was devout, stern and strict about books: novels wasted time, he thought, and science books were suspect. David loved books about travel and science, and father and son fought a long, quiet battle over it. The last time his father beat him, David remembered, was for refusing to read a dull religious book that seemed to set faith against the study of nature. His mother, Agnes, was small, neat and cheerful, and made a tea-seller’s income stretch. Sometimes, at midnight, she came and took the book out of his hands so that he would go to bed.

The family treasured one story. An ancestor on the Hebridean island of Ulva, dying, told his children he had searched the family’s whole history and never found a dishonest man in it. He left them one rule: “Be honest.” Of all his family’s traditions, David said, that was the only one he felt proud of. Later in life people accused him of being stubborn and hard. Almost nobody accused him of being dishonest about money.

In 1823, at ten, David went into the mill as a piecer. His job was to walk up and down beside the spinning machines and join the threads when they broke, reaching in among the moving parts without stopping them. The day ran from six in the morning to eight at night, with short breaks for meals, in heat and noise and air thick with cotton dust. He did it for ten years. Say it plainly: that system used up children for profit. Livingstone never complained about it, and later called it a school. Both things are true.

With part of his first week’s wages he bought a Latin grammar. After work he went to the mill’s night school from eight until ten, then studied at home until midnight or later. At the mill he propped a book on the machine and caught a sentence at a time as he passed. It taught him to concentrate anywhere; years later he could read and write in the middle of a shouting crowd. On free days he went collecting plants, rocks and fossil shells.

The mill gave him two things he would need in Africa: endurance, and respect for working people. He was often more at ease with porters than with officials. It also gave him something less helpful. In a mill, you are what you produce. Livingstone came to judge everyone by how hard they worked, and he despised people who couldn’t keep up. Endurance is a gift. Patience with weaker people is a gift too, and it is much harder to learn at a spinning machine.

One more detail. Much of the cotton spun at Blantyre had been grown by enslaved people in the American South. Young David didn’t think about that. But the idea that Africans might grow cotton to sell, instead of being sold themselves, would one day shape his whole life.

Ecclesiastes says to work with all your might, not because work always succeeds, but because life is short. Livingstone lived that verse. Paul adds: work “as unto the Lord, and not unto men.” Working hard isn’t the same as working for God, and it took Livingstone a lifetime to learn the difference.

Maybe you are the one who always works hardest, and you quietly look down on people who don’t. Or maybe you are carrying a load nobody your age should have to carry. Either way, God sees the work, and the worker.

One thing to do this week: notice one person this week who can’t keep up with you, in a class, a team or at home. Instead of getting impatient, help them once, without making a point of it.

fields.title: Slow of Speech
fields.body_html:
“And Moses said unto Jehovah, Oh, Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” — Exodus 4:10 (ASV)

David grew up knowing the gospel. His parents taught it to him, and he could explain the doctrines as well as any boy in Blantyre. But in his late teens, he wrote, he began to feel for the first time his own need of what Christ had done on the cross, and to take it personally. There was no dramatic night and no famous preacher. A truth he already believed became his own.

Something had held him back. His father’s church seemed suspicious of science, and David loved rocks and stars. He thought he might have to choose between his Bible and his questions. Then he read a book by Thomas Dick, a Scottish minister and amateur astronomer, who argued that the universe is God’s handiwork and studying it is a kind of worship. The wall David had imagined wasn’t there. He could love both, because they had the same Maker.

He described the change with a picture from medicine. It was as if someone colour-blind were suddenly cured. Nothing new appeared, but the whole world looked different. The doctrines had colour now. So did creation. And so did other people’s needs. Soon, he wrote, he resolved to give his life to relieving human misery.

An appeal from a missionary in China asked for doctors, and David decided to become one. In 1836, at twenty-three, he began studying medicine and chemistry in Glasgow, paying his own fees, living in a cheap room and walking the eight miles home at weekends. In summer he went back to the mill to earn the next winter’s money. He wasn’t brilliant. He just kept working after everyone else had stopped.

He applied to the London Missionary Society. He liked that it sent out, in its own words, no particular church system, only the gospel of Christ. He didn’t want to export a Scottish denomination. He wanted to preach Christ.

In 1838 the Society sent him to Chipping Ongar, in Essex, to train under a minister named Richard Cecil. He nearly failed. He was shy and awkward, his accent was thick, and his public prayers were halting. Cecil reported that he was sensible and good-tempered but heavy in manner, and asked for his probation to be extended.

His first biographer told a story from those who knew him at Ongar. Sent to preach in a village chapel, David learned his sermon by heart, climbed into the pulpit, read out his text, and found his mind completely empty. After a painful silence, he told the people he had forgotten everything he meant to say, came down, and left the chapel.

Another student remembered something else, though only at second hand. Walking back from London one night, David found a woman who had been thrown from a carriage. He carried her to a house and made sure she was cared for, then got lost and reached Ongar at dawn, worn out. He couldn’t preach the Good Samaritan from memory. He could be one on a dark country road.

In 1839 the Society accepted him. He never became a good preacher. Years later, famous, he read his speeches badly and hated giving them.

Moses told God he couldn’t speak. God didn’t make him eloquent. He said, “Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth.” Livingstone was never made eloquent either. God needed him to walk, to write and to tell the world what he had seen, and he was given gifts for that.

Maybe there is one thing you are bad at that everyone else seems to find easy: speaking up, reading aloud, making friends. It doesn’t disqualify you. God may have given you something else to do.

One thing to do this week: write down one weakness you think makes you useless to God. Next to it, write one thing you can do. Then do that thing for someone this week.

fields.title: The Lion at Mabotsa
fields.body_html:
“But the Lord stood by me, and strengthened me; that through me the message might be fully proclaimed, and that all the Gentiles might hear: and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.” — 2 Timothy 4:17 (ASV)

In 1839 war between Britain and China, over Britain’s opium trade, closed China to him. In London he met Robert Moffat, the most famous missionary in Britain, who had worked for years at Kuruman in southern Africa. Moffat later remembered telling him not to settle at an old station but to push north, where he had seen the smoke of a thousand villages with no missionary. That phrase comes from Moffat’s memory years afterwards, so hold it lightly. What is certain is that Moffat pointed him north, and he went.

On his last morning at home in 1840, David read Psalm 121 at family worship. His father walked with him to Glasgow. They never saw each other again. He was ordained, sailed in December, learned to fix his position by the stars from the ship’s captain, and in July 1841 reached Kuruman.

He was disappointed. Fewer people lived there than he had imagined, and he thought too many missionaries were crowded in the south. It was a typical judgement: partly right, partly unfair. He didn’t see what twenty years of work had cost. He saw what hadn’t been done.

So he went north. He spent about six months living among the Bakwena people, hearing no English, so that he would have to learn Setswana properly. He treated the sick, helped dig a water channel, and listened. Out of this came one of his best ideas: that Africa would be reached with the gospel mainly by African Christians, not by a few foreigners. History proved him right. He didn’t always act on it, and his books gave too little credit to the African Christians who did much of the work.

He liked the people he met. He wrote, against fashionable racist theories, that Africans were in no way inferior to Europeans in natural ability. But he saw almost nothing good in their religion or customs, and he assumed that becoming Christian meant living like a Scottish working family. He saw people more clearly than most Europeans of his time. Not as clearly as he thought.

In 1843 he helped start a station at Mabotsa, among the Bakgatla people. Lions were killing their cattle. In February 1844 he went out with the men to hunt one. He fired both barrels into a lion and was reloading when he heard a shout. “Starting, and looking half round,” he wrote, “I saw the lion just in the act of springing upon me.” It caught him by the shoulder and shook him like a terrier with a rat. Strangely, he said, he felt no pain or terror, only a kind of dreaminess.

Then the lion turned. A Christian teacher from Kuruman named Mebalwe had run up and fired at it. Both barrels of his gun failed. The lion sprang on Mebalwe and bit him in the thigh. Another man ran at it with a spear and was mauled too. Then the lion dropped dead from Livingstone’s earlier shots.

Notice whose courage saved his life. Mebalwe ran towards a lion with a gun that didn’t work. In the old retellings he is often left out. This will happen again and again in this story: Livingstone survived because of Africans whose names his books barely mention.

His arm was crushed, set badly by his own directions, and never healed straight. He went to Kuruman to recover. The Moffats were back from Britain, with their eldest daughter, Mary, twenty-three, who had grown up in Africa and spoke Setswana from childhood. In January 1845 they married.

Paul said God rescued him “out of the mouth of the lion” so that the message could be preached. Livingstone believed he had been spared for a purpose. That belief carried him through many dangers. At times it also made him reckless.

One thing to do this week: think of someone whose help made a difference to you but who never got any credit. Thank them, by name, this week.

study_questions.question: Who saved Livingstone from the lion?
study_questions.answer: Mebalwe, a Christian teacher from Kuruman, who ran at the lion with a gun that misfired and was bitten himself, and another man who attacked it with a spear.

study_questions.question: Why did Livingstone live for six months among the Bakwena?
study_questions.answer: To hear no English and learn Setswana and the people’s way of life properly. It helped him in all his later dealings with them.

study_questions.question: What was one of his best ideas about mission?
study_questions.answer: That the gospel would spread through Africa mainly by African Christians, not foreign missionaries. Later history proved him right.

fields.title: Sechele
fields.body_html:
“And Philip ran to him, and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest? And he said, How can I, except some one shall guide me? And he besought Philip to come up and sit with him.” — Acts 8:30-31 (ASV)

Livingstone quarrelled with Rogers Edwards, the older missionary at Mabotsa. Rather than keep fighting, he gave up the house he had built and in 1845 moved with Mary to Chonuane, the town of the Bakwena and their chief, Sechele, who had asked him to come.

Sechele was about Livingstone’s age: tall, clever, forceful. His father had been murdered when he was a boy, and he had grown up a refugee before winning back his place as chief. He was a hunter, a politician and, by custom, a rainmaker, responsible for bringing the rain everyone depended on. He had several wives, as chiefs did, and through them alliances with leading families.

He learned the alphabet on the first day. Soon he was reading the Bible hungrily. His favourite book was Isaiah; Isaiah, he said, was a fine man who knew how to speak. He sat so long over his books that, Livingstone noted with amusement, he grew stout.

Sechele asked hard questions. Hearing about the coming judgement, he said, “You startle me: these words make all my bones to shake.” Then he asked why, if Livingstone’s ancestors had known these things, they had not sent word sooner. His own ancestors, he said, had all passed into darkness without knowing where they were going. Livingstone had no satisfying answer. There isn’t one that removes the force of that question. It was grief for his own people, and a rebuke to a church that took eighteen centuries to reach the Bakwena.

Sechele thought like a chief. Once he believed, he offered to call his headmen with their whips of rhinoceros hide and make everyone believe together. Livingstone refused, and he was right: faith can’t be beaten into anyone. But Sechele was also telling him something true. Among the Bakwena, a chief’s religion was never private. If he changed, everything changed.

In 1847 the town moved to Kolobeng, by a river. Then the rains failed, year after year. The river dried up. Many Bakwena drew the obvious conclusion: their chief had dropped the rain rites for the missionary’s religion, and the rain had stopped. Livingstone later wrote an imagined debate between a doctor and a rain doctor, and let the rain doctor have some of the best lines.

Sechele asked to be baptised. The mission would not baptise a man with more than one wife. Sechele understood the cost far better than Livingstone did. These women were his wives by his people’s law, the mothers of his children, the daughters of powerful families. In the end he kept his first wife and sent the others home with their goods and a message that he had nothing against them; he was following God’s word. He was baptised on 1 October 1848. The town was dismayed. Nobody asked the women.

Early in 1849 it came out that one of his former wives was pregnant by him. Livingstone suspended him from communion. As far as we know, Sechele is the only African Livingstone ever baptised.

But that isn’t the end. Sechele didn’t give up his faith. He kept reading the Bible, held worship for his people, invited other missionaries, and preached himself until he died in 1892. The Bakwena became Christian largely through him. The man Livingstone suspended became the evangelist of his own people.

In Acts, after the baptism, Philip disappears and the African official goes home rejoicing, to do what Philip never could. It was the same with Sechele. Livingstone left thinking he had failed. He was wrong.

You might think one stumble means someone is finished, or that you are. God doesn’t write people off that fast.

fields.title: Without Water
fields.body_html:
“The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.” — Isaiah 35:1 (ASV)

North of Kolobeng lay the Kalahari, the dry country the Batswana called the thirstland. African hunters and travellers had crossed it for generations, and the San and Bakgalagadi peoples lived in it. Beyond it, people said, was a great lake, and beyond that the kingdom of Sebetwane, leader of the Makololo, who had once helped Sechele win back his chieftaincy.

In 1849 Livingstone crossed the desert with two English hunters, guided by Ramotobi, a Bakwena man Sechele sent. They reached Lake Ngami. The people living beside it had known it all their lives, but in London it counted as a discovery, and Livingstone won a geography prize. It was the beginning of a change in how he saw his work.

In 1850 he took his family: Mary, who was pregnant, and their three small children. The children caught fever and they turned back. Soon afterwards Mary gave birth to a daughter, Elizabeth, who lived about six weeks. Mary was left partly paralysed in her face and worn out.

Her mother, Mary Moffat, heard that Livingstone meant to take her daughter north again, pregnant again, in 1851. She wrote him a fierce letter about his recklessness with his wife and children. Nothing in it was unfair. He went anyway.

On that journey their guide, a San man named Shobo, lost the way. For four days there was no water. Livingstone feared the children would die of thirst in front of them. He wrote that it would almost have been a relief to be blamed, but Mary said not a word of reproach, though her eyes showed her agony. On the fifth day some of the men found water. The children lived.

That is the most honest thing he ever wrote about his marriage. He knew he was to blame. He knew she knew. He was grateful she didn’t say so. And he didn’t change course. You might ask whether her silence was strength, or just exhaustion.

In June 1851 they reached the Makololo on the Chobe River. Sebetwane, who had fought his way north across the Kalahari decades before and built a kingdom of many peoples, welcomed them warmly. Livingstone called him the finest African chief he had ever met. Two weeks later Sebetwane died of a chest illness. His son Sekeletu, about eighteen, took his place.

Then Livingstone reached a great river, the upper Zambezi, flowing far into the middle of Africa. He began to dream of it as a highway. And he saw something that changed his life. Traders from the west coast were buying captives from the Makololo with guns and cloth, to sell on. For the first time he was looking at the slave trade. He decided that if honest traders could buy ivory and other goods instead, the market for human beings would collapse. It was a sincere idea, born of what he saw. Later, other people would use it for very different ends.

He could not take his family into the fever country, and he would not give up the north. So in April 1852 he put Mary and their four children on a ship to Britain. He would not see them for four and a half years.

Isaiah pictures a highway through the desert for God’s people coming home, and the desert bursting into flower. Livingstone saw himself as a road-builder for God. But the prophet’s highway is God’s, not ours. On the way to building his road, Livingstone left his family by the side of it. The desert hadn’t blossomed for Mary. It had nearly killed her children.

Big dreams can be good. But a dream that costs the people closest to you everything, without asking them, needs a second look.

One thing to do this week: ask someone in your family what one of your plans or habits costs them. Listen without defending yourself. Then decide whether anything should change.

study_questions.answer: Traders buying captives from the Makololo to sell on. It was his first sight of the slave trade, and he resolved to fight it by opening honest trade.

study_questions.answer: He took Mary and the children into danger against warnings, and then sent them to Britain for years, so that they paid much of the cost of his calling.

fields.title: Kolobeng Plundered
fields.body_html:
“God is our refuge and strength, A very present help in trouble.” — Psalm 46:1 (ASV)

East of Kolobeng, Afrikaner settlers known as the Boers had set up their own republics on land taken from African peoples, and they demanded African labour. Missionaries accused them of taking African children as so-called apprentices who were little different from slaves. The Boers, for their part, accused missionaries of arming Africans against them. In Livingstone’s case it was partly true: he had repaired guns for Sechele, believing a people who could defend themselves would not be enslaved. In 1852 Britain signed a treaty recognising the Boer republics, and the Bakwena were left on their own.

In August 1852, while Livingstone was still travelling north from the Cape, a Boer commando attacked Sechele’s people at their hill stronghold of Dimawe. Livingstone reported that about sixty Bakwena were killed and more than two hundred women and children carried off. The Bakwena fought hard, and afterwards counted the battle a victory, because they had not been destroyed. But their town was burned. At Kolobeng, Livingstone’s house was plundered, his books torn up, his medicines smashed.

The house mattered less than the people. In 1853 Sechele set out to ask Queen Victoria in person for protection. He reached Cape Town and made sworn statements about the attack, but his money ran out and nobody would pay his passage. He went home, rebuilt his town in a new place, made his own peace with the Boers, and became one of the most powerful chiefs in the region. His help didn’t come from London. It came from his own skill and his people’s resilience.

Meanwhile Mary and the four children had landed in Britain with almost no money and nowhere to live. Mary had grown up in Africa and had few friends there. Staying with Livingstone’s family didn’t work out, and she moved out. For four years she drifted between rented rooms in different towns, living on a small allowance from the mission, often ill, often lonely. Her husband’s letters were few, because there was no way to send them from the interior. Some of her friends and relatives believed she began drinking heavily in those years. That can’t be proved, and it shouldn’t be said as fact. What is clear is that she was deeply unhappy and felt abandoned, and there are hints that her faith was shaken. Robert, the eldest, grew up angry. All the children grew up without a father.

The Victorian biographies hurried past this. We shouldn’t. Livingstone didn’t mean to neglect them. He sent them to safety, but without the means to live safely, and without himself, for a journey he could have postponed. Paul is blunt about people who don’t provide for their own household. A Christian story can’t call this courage without also calling it failure.

In 1853 Livingstone reached the Makololo town of Linyanti, and Sekeletu welcomed him. He looked for a healthy place for a mission and found only low, wet, fever country. He preached; people listened politely. Sekeletu told him frankly that he didn’t want to learn to read the Bible in case it changed his heart and left him with only one wife, like Sechele. The story had travelled north.

Around this time Livingstone wrote in his journal a resolution to place no value on anything he had, except as it related to the kingdom of Christ. It is a noble resolution, and he mostly lived it. But it raises a question. Did his wife and children count, in his mind, among the things he could give away for the kingdom? He would have been horrified at the idea. His choices suggest they did.

The psalm says God is a very present help in trouble. It doesn’t promise the city won’t be attacked. Sechele’s people knew that. So did a lonely woman in a rented room.

Some of the hardest suffering happens out of sight, in kitchens and rented rooms, not on battlefields. God sees it.

One thing to do this week: think of someone in your life who is carrying a hidden load, maybe a parent, a sibling or a friend. Do one practical thing this week to make it lighter.

study_questions.question: What did Sechele do after the attack on Dimawe?
study_questions.answer: He tried to reach Queen Victoria to ask for protection, got as far as Cape Town, then went home, rebuilt his town and became one of the most powerful chiefs in the region.

study_questions.question: What was life like for Mary Livingstone in Britain?
study_questions.answer: She moved between rented rooms for four years with four children, little money and few friends, often ill and lonely, and felt abandoned.

study_questions.question: Why wouldn’t Sekeletu learn to read the Bible?
study_questions.answer: He was afraid it might change his heart and leave him with only one wife, as had happened to Sechele.

fields.title: Twenty-Seven Men
fields.body_html:
“In whose eyes a reprobate is despised, But who honoreth them that fear Jehovah; He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.” — Psalm 15:4 (ASV)

On 11 November 1853, Livingstone left Linyanti for the Atlantic coast with twenty-seven men. They weren’t his servants. Sekeletu chose them from the many peoples of his kingdom, and they went because their chief sent them and because they hoped to open a trade route to the sea. Their leader was a man named Pitsane. This is often called Livingstone’s journey. It was theirs as much as his. Without them he wouldn’t have got a hundred miles.

He took almost nothing: a few clothes, a small tent, a gun, beads to pay for food, a sextant, a Bible, and a magic lantern, an early projector with painted glass slides of Bible stories. He depended on the goodwill of the people whose land he passed through.

The rains came. The paths flooded and the party was soaked day and night. Livingstone had fever after fever, and grew so weak he could barely sit on his riding ox.

Among the Lunda peoples they met a young woman chief named Manenko, a niece of the great chief Shinte. She overruled Livingstone’s plans, insisted on escorting them to her uncle herself, and marched at the head of the column through pouring rain faster than the men could keep up. Livingstone was annoyed and impressed. For those few days, he wasn’t the main character in the story. She was.

Further west, near the Kasai River, the Chiboque surrounded the party and demanded a man, an ox, a gun or a tusk as the price of passage. A man meant one of his companions, to be sold as a slave. Livingstone sat on his camp stool with his gun across his knees, his men pressed close around him, and refused to hand over anyone. In the end he gave an ox, and no blood was shed. Another time some of his own exhausted men nearly mutinied, and he ran out of his tent with a pistol and threatened the ringleader. He was a leader who could frighten as well as inspire.

At the Kwango River, a Portuguese militia sergeant named Cypriano di Abreu, whose mother was African, helped them across and fed them generously. On 31 May 1854 they walked into Luanda, capital of the Portuguese colony of Angola. Livingstone could barely stand.

The men had never seen the sea. Livingstone recorded what they said: they had always believed what the old people told them, that the world had no end, but now the world had told them it was finished, and there was no more of it.

Luanda had been one of the biggest slave ports in the world for over two centuries. Livingstone looked at its fine houses and knew what had paid for them. A British official, Edmund Gabriel, nursed him through months of illness. The men earned money unloading coal from ships.

Then came a choice. British naval officers offered Livingstone a passage home to England. He hadn’t seen his family in over two years. He was ill and worn out, and he had done what he came to do. Nobody would have blamed him.

He refused. He had promised Sekeletu he would bring the men home. They didn’t know the way back, and the country was full of slave traders who would happily seize an unprotected group. He believed that if he left, they would never see the Zambezi again. The ship he would have sailed on sank off Madeira, with his journal and maps aboard.

Psalm 15 describes the person God welcomes as someone who “sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not”: who keeps a promise even when it costs. Livingstone kept this one at the cost of two more years in Africa. It is one of the finest things he ever did.

It’s uncomfortable, though. The man who wouldn’t abandon twenty-seven men on a strange coast had left his wife alone in English lodgings. Keep both facts. Don’t smooth either away.

One thing to do this week: think of a promise you’ve made that has become inconvenient to keep. Keep it this week, even if it costs you something.

study_questions.question: Who were the twenty-seven men?
study_questions.answer: Men from the many peoples of Sekeletu’s kingdom, chosen by their chief and led by Pitsane, who went to open a trade route to the sea. They were not Livingstone’s servants.

study_questions.question: Why did Livingstone refuse to sail home from Luanda?
study_questions.answer: He had promised Sekeletu to bring the men home, and he believed they would not survive the journey back without him.

study_questions.question: What did the men say when they first saw the sea?
study_questions.answer: That they had always believed the world had no end, but now the world had told them it was finished and there was no more of it.

fields.title: The Word of a Gentleman
fields.body_html:
“And Jesus came to them and spake unto them, saying, All authority hath been given unto me in heaven and on earth. Go ye therefore, and make disciples of all the nations … and lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.” — Matthew 28:18-20 (ASV)

The way back took a year. Livingstone rewrote the journal that had sunk, and the men carried home the goods they had earned. In September 1855 they walked into Linyanti as heroes, telling everyone they had gone to the end of the world. Their faithfulness made Livingstone a trusted man among the Makololo.

The western route was too long and unhealthy, so he tried east, down the Zambezi to the Indian Ocean. In November 1855 he set out with more than a hundred men from Sekeletu, and a guide and interpreter named Sekwebu, who knew the languages of the east.

He had heard of a great waterfall the people called Mosi-oa-Tunya, “the smoke that thunders.” Sekeletu’s men paddled him to an island on the very edge of it, and he lay down and looked into the gorge. He wrote that scenes so lovely must have been gazed on by angels. Then he named it after Queen Victoria.

That moment says a lot. The falls had a name already. The people living nearby had known them for centuries, and they were the ones who brought him there. He meant the new name as an honour. But it fits a habit of mind, his and his country’s, in which what Africans knew didn’t count until a European wrote it down. Today the national park around the falls is called Mosi-oa-Tunya.

On the high, cool plateau north of the river he saw what he thought was healthy country for missions. The vision that would drive the next eight years of his life was born there.

On 14 January 1856 the party reached the point where the Luangwa River joins the Zambezi. Large numbers of armed people gathered on the far bank, and Livingstone’s men expected to be attacked when they crossed. That night he wrote in his journal one of the most famous entries of his life.

He admitted to great turmoil of spirit. All his plans might be wiped out the next day, he wrote, by the people across the river, whom he called by a contemptuous word his age used. Then he read Jesus’ promise to be with his disciples always, to the end of the world. That, he wrote, was the word of a gentleman of the strictest honour, and it settled the matter. He would not sneak across by night. He would take his star readings, though they might be his last. He felt quite calm now, and thanked God.

Notice two things. First, his faith and his prejudice sat in the same paragraph. fields.title: “I Never Made a Sacrifice”
fields.body_html:
“For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed to us-ward.” — Romans 8:18 (ASV)

In December 1856 Livingstone landed in England after sixteen years away. His children hardly knew him. His father had died that February. And he was suddenly the most famous man in Britain. He met the Queen, received honours, and drew crowds everywhere, though he read his speeches badly and hated the attention. His book, Missionary Travels, sold some seventy thousand copies. For the first time in his life, he had money.

The missionary society was less thrilled. Their missionary had spent years exploring instead of preaching. Livingstone was offended; he believed everything he did opened a way for the gospel. When the government offered him a post as consul and the leadership of an expedition up the Zambezi, he resigned from the society. He insisted he was still a missionary. From now on, though, he was paid by the government.

On 4 December 1857 he spoke to a packed hall at Cambridge University. “People talk of the sacrifice I have made in spending so much of my life in Africa,” he said. “Can that be called a sacrifice which is simply paid back as a small part of a great debt owing to our God, which we can never repay?” And: “It is emphatically no sacrifice. Say rather it is a privilege.” He finished that passage with the words that became famous: “I never made a sacrifice.”

He was echoing Paul: present suffering isn’t worth comparing with the glory to come. It’s true, and it was sincere. But hear it alongside the last four years. Livingstone hadn’t made a sacrifice, he said. Mary had, in her rented rooms. The children had. Sekwebu had. Much of the cost of his calling was paid by other people.

He ended with an appeal: “I go back to Africa to try to make an open path for commerce and Christianity.” Students from Cambridge and Oxford answered by founding a new mission to Central Africa. Later, his phrase was stretched into a slogan, “Christianity, commerce and civilisation,” and used by people who cared nothing for Christ to justify taking over Africa. He didn’t mean conquest. He believed Africans should keep their land and govern themselves, and he attacked the Boers and the Portuguese for seizing both. But he believed British trade was basically Christian and good, and he underestimated how fast trade turns into exploitation when one side has the guns and ships. Jesus said, “Ye cannot serve God and mammon.” Livingstone thought he could harness money for God. It’s harder than it looks.

In 1858 the Zambezi Expedition set out. Mary came, but she was pregnant again and stayed at Kuruman, where their daughter Anna Mary was born. The expedition’s steamer was so feeble that canoes paddled past it.

Then came Kebrabasa. On his way down in 1856 Livingstone had walked round a stretch of the river where he had been told there were rapids, and assumed a steamer could get through. In November 1858 he went to look. The whole river forced its way through a narrow, rocky gorge in rapids and falls. No steamer could pass. His colleague John Kirk saw it at once. Livingstone wouldn’t accept it, and asked the government for a stronger boat. The great plan, the river highway, was blocked by something he hadn’t seen because he had walked round it.

He was a hard leader of Europeans. He took disagreement as disloyalty. He dismissed the young geologist Richard Thornton, and he sent home the artist Thomas Baines in disgrace after his brother Charles accused Baines of theft, without giving him a real hearing. Baines denied it all his life, and historians have generally believed him. Neither man ever got an apology.

The same stubbornness that carried him across Africa made it almost impossible for him to say “I was wrong.” Sometimes perseverance is faith. Sometimes it’s just pride.

One thing to do this week: think of one time recently you were wrong but didn’t admit it. Go to the person this week and say so, plainly, without excuses.

study_questions.question: What did Livingstone mean by “I never made a sacrifice”?

study_questions.question: What is missing from that statement?
study_questions.answer: The cost others paid: Mary’s years alone, his children growing up without him, and Africans like Sekwebu who died on his journeys.

study_questions.question: Why was Kebrabasa such a blow?

fields.title: Shupanga
fields.body_html:
“Jehovah is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart, And saveth such as are of a contrite spirit.” — Psalm 34:18 (ASV)

Blocked at Kebrabasa, Livingstone turned up the Shire River. Above it he found cool, fertile highlands and, in 1859, the great Lake Nyasa, now Lake Malawi. Local people and traders had long known it; he was the first to report it to the wider world. He also found one of the main slave routes of East Africa running right through it.

In 1861 the new Universities’ Mission arrived, led by a cheerful, brave young bishop named Charles Mackenzie. In July, walking into the highlands with him, Livingstone’s party reached the village of a chief named Mbame. A long line of captives came in: men with their necks locked in heavy forked sticks, women and children roped together. When the drivers saw the Englishmen, they ran. The party cut the ropes and sawed through the sticks. Eighty-four people, most of them women and children, were told they were free. They described the march: a woman killed because she couldn’t carry both her load and her baby, and the baby killed with her.

Among the children freed in those weeks, by the usual account, was a Yao boy of about ten named Chuma. Remember his name.

Jesus began his ministry reading Isaiah’s words about “liberty to the captives.” At Mbame’s village, for once, freedom from sin and freedom from chains didn’t have to be argued about. It was both.

Then things turned dark. Yao groups, themselves driven from their homes, were raiding the local Mang’anja villages for captives. Days later Livingstone’s party clashed with a raiding band and several raiders were killed. It was the first time he had led men into a fight where people died, and it troubled him deeply. Then he went back to the river. Mackenzie, left among people being killed and enslaved, went with Mang’anja forces against the raiders. People in Britain were outraged that a bishop had gone to war. It is hard to judge either man. Doing nothing wasn’t innocent either.

Livingstone arranged to meet Mackenzie at the mouth of the Ruo River in January 1862, and didn’t make it; his boat ran aground. Mackenzie waited on an island in the rainy season, his medicines lost when his canoe overturned. He died of fever on 31 January. Some never forgave Livingstone. He said he couldn’t help it. Both were true.

Mary arrived at the end of January 1862. She had left the children, including baby Anna Mary, in Scotland and come because she couldn’t bear being apart any longer. She was no frail visitor: she was a missionary’s daughter who had grown up among the Batswana, spoke Setswana from childhood, ran schools, nursed the sick and crossed the desert twice while pregnant. People called her Ma-Robert, mother of Robert.

For a few weeks at Shupanga, beside the Zambezi, they were together. In April she caught fever. The usual treatments failed. On 27 April 1862, with her husband beside her, she died. She was forty-one. They buried her under a great baobab tree.

Livingstone was shattered. His journal, as his biographer printed it, said it was the first heavy blow he had suffered, and that it took away all his strength. He had loved her when he married her, he wrote, and loved her more the longer they lived together. For the first time in his life, he felt willing to die.

Some of his letters defended him: she had insisted on coming. Others let something else slip through: she came because he had left her alone so long. It would be cruel to blame him for malaria. It would be dishonest not to say that the shape of her lonely married life came from his choices.

The psalm says God is near the broken-hearted and saves the contrite, people whose grief sees their own part in the wound. There are hints of that in his journal. Within days, though, he was back at work.

One thing to do this week: if you have hurt someone close to you, don’t only feel bad about it. Tell God plainly what your part was, then tell the person.

study_questions.answer: Livingstone’s party freed eighty-four captives, mostly women and children, by cutting their ropes and sawing through the slave-sticks. Chuma was probably freed in those weeks.

study_questions.answer: A missionary’s daughter raised among the Batswana who spoke Setswana, ran schools, nursed the sick and crossed the desert twice while pregnant. People called her Ma-Robert.

fields.title: The Sentence of Death
fields.body_html:
“By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out unto a place which he was to receive for an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.” — Hebrews 11:8 (ASV)

When Livingstone went back up the Shire at the end of 1862, the valley he had praised as the most promising place in Central Africa had become a graveyard. Drought had destroyed the harvests, and slave raiders had burned the villages and carried off thousands of people. Bodies floated past the steamer every day. The drought and raids had their own causes, but the valley he had hoped to save was ruined within a few years.

In 1863 the government recalled the expedition. As far as they could see, it had produced a blocked river, a dead bishop, a failed mission and a string of resignations. Livingstone accepted it, deeply hurt.

He wouldn’t sell the small steamer he had paid for where it might be used in the slave trade, so in 1864 he sailed it across the Indian Ocean to Bombay, two and a half thousand miles, in a river boat never meant for the open sea, with a crew that included young African men who had never been to sea, among them Chuma. It was brave, and reckless with other people’s lives.

In London he heard about his eldest son. Robert, eighteen, angry and resentful of his absent father, had gone to America and joined the Union army in the Civil War under a false name, so as not to shame his family. He was captured and died in a prison camp in North Carolina in December 1864. Livingstone wrote his children loving letters, but he was rarely there, and stern when he was. Paul wrote, “And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath.” Robert was provoked. His father seems to have blamed Robert more than himself.

In 1865 his mother died, and in August he left Britain for the last time. The Royal Geographical Society wanted him to settle the source of the Nile. He agreed on one condition: he would go as a missionary, and do geography on the way. He also meant to see the slave routes and expose them.

In 1866 he landed on the coast of what is now Tanzania. Among his party were Susi, a man from Shupanga who had worked on the Zambezi, and Chuma and his friend Wikatani, the two boys freed in the Shire Highlands, now young men.

The road inland was a slave road. Day after day he wrote down what he saw: a woman tied by the neck to a tree and left dead, people killed when they couldn’t keep up. He wrote it plainly, as evidence, so Britain would act.

Near Lake Nyasa, Wikatani found relatives he thought were lost, and stayed with them. Then a group of the party deserted out of fear and, to excuse themselves, told the authorities at Zanzibar that Livingstone had been killed. Obituaries appeared in Britain before a search party proved the story false.

On 20 January 1867 two porters ran off with his medicine chest, including the quinine that kept him alive. He wrote that he felt he had received the sentence of death, as Bishop Mackenzie had. It was nearly true. Fever attacked him again and again.

He didn’t turn back. Without medicine, money or enough men, he could only survive by travelling with the Arab-Swahili caravans from Zanzibar that dealt in ivory and slaves, among them the trader later called Tippu Tip. He ate their food and accepted their protection, while writing down what they did. The man who freed captives at Mbame’s now depended on slavers to stay alive. He wasn’t part of their trade. But he knew how it looked.

He reached Lake Tanganyika, Lake Mweru and then Lake Bangweulu, which no European had described before, and became convinced the rivers there fed the Nile. He was wrong; they fed the Congo.

Abraham went out “not knowing whither he went.” Livingstone didn’t know whether he would live, or whether anyone knew he was still alive. He went on anyway.

One thing to do this week: write a real letter or message to a parent or someone older in your family, saying one thing you are grateful for and one thing you wish you could talk about. Send it, or pray about whether to.

study_questions.question: What happened to Robert Livingstone?
study_questions.answer: Angry and unsettled, he joined the Union army in America under a false name, was captured, and died in a Confederate prison camp in 1864.

study_questions.question: Why did losing the medicine chest matter so much?
study_questions.answer: It held his quinine, his only defence against malaria. He wrote that he felt he had received the sentence of death.

fields.title: How Long?
fields.body_html:
“O Jehovah, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear? I cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save.” — Habakkuk 1:2 (ASV)

West of Lake Tanganyika lay Manyema, the new frontier of the ivory and slave trade. Its people had no guns, and the traders took ivory by trade where they could and by force where they couldn’t. Livingstone liked the people and wrote about their gardens, markets and courtesy. He didn’t doubt that they had done nothing to deserve what was being done to them.

These were the most miserable years of his life. In 1870 his feet broke out in ulcers that ate into the flesh, and he was laid up for months in a hut. Most of his porters deserted. For a time only three people stayed: Susi, Chuma, and a young man named Gardner, who nursed him and found him food. With nothing else to read, he read the Bible through four times.

In March 1871 he reached Nyangwe, a market town on the great river he believed was the Nile. On 15 July he went to the market as usual. Hundreds of people had come to buy and sell, most of them women. A quarrel broke out. Then the armed men of a trader named Dugumbe opened fire into the crowd. People ran for the river; canoes overturned in the crush; the gunmen kept shooting at people in the water, then crossed and burned the villages on the far side. Livingstone estimated three or four hundred dead, most of them women.

He could do nothing. He wrote what he saw, heard the wailing from across the river, and wrote a short prayer for God’s kingdom to come. It is the Lord’s Prayer, prayed as a cry of protest.

Habakkuk cried the same thing: how long? He got no explanation, only a promise that the earth would one day be filled with the knowledge of God’s glory. Livingstone got no explanation either. But his account reached Britain in 1872, shocked the public, and added to the pressure that closed the great slave market at Zanzibar.

There is a harder part. In our own century, scholars used special imaging to read his faded original diary from 1871, written on scraps of newspaper. It shows that before the massacre he had been living under the protection of traders, including men linked to Dugumbe, and that his own hired men had been violent towards local people. The published version made him a purely horrified onlooker. He didn’t lie about the massacre, and he didn’t cause it. But the story was shaped to put more distance between him and the traders than there really was. That’s very human. It isn’t the whole truth.

He turned back to Ujiji, sick and broken. He reached it in late October 1871, by his own confused reckoning, and found the supplies left for him had been sold off.

Then Susi came running. He had seen an Englishman. Henry Morton Stanley, a journalist sent by a New York newspaper, marched in with a large caravan. In his own account, Stanley walked up, took off his hat, and said, “Dr. Livingstone, I presume?” Those words come from Stanley alone. The pages of his diary for those days are missing, his versions differ, and even the date is uncertain. What is certain is that they met, and the meeting saved Livingstone’s life.

Stanley brought food, medicine and letters, and begged him to come home. Livingstone refused; he had to finish. Stanley left in March 1872, weeping. That year Livingstone wrote a prayer for Heaven’s blessing on anyone, of any nation, who would help “to heal this open sore of the world.” On his fifty-ninth birthday he wrote: “Birthday. My Jesus, my king, my life, my all; I again dedicate my whole self to Thee.” He asked God to let him finish his task.

In August 1872 men arrived to join him, among them Jacob Wainwright, about twenty, a Yao by birth who had been freed from slave traders as a boy and educated in India.

One thing to do this week: when you see news of violence that makes you feel helpless, don’t scroll past. Pray Habakkuk’s honest “how long?” and then do one small thing: give, write, or speak up.

fields.title: Faithful Hands
fields.body_html:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a grain of wheat fall into the earth and die, it abideth by itself alone; but if it die, it beareth much fruit.” — John 12:24 (ASV)

His last company numbered over sixty people. At its heart were Susi and Chuma. With them were young men from the school in India, among them Jacob Wainwright, Carus Farrar and Matthew Wellington; a boy named Majwara who slept at Livingstone’s door; women including Halima, who cooked for him; and porters from the coast. In the coming months, these people would decide what happened to David Livingstone, living and dead.

From January to April 1873 they waded through the flooded swamps around Lake Bangweulu, often waist-deep, in rain, with leeches. Livingstone was bleeding badly and could no longer walk. The men carried him on a litter. On 27 April he wrote his last entry: “Knocked up quite, and remain—recover—sent to buy milch-goats.” Two days later they carried him to the village of a chief named Chitambo, in what is now Zambia, and built him a hut.

What we know of that night comes from the men, as they later told it. Around midnight he called Susi, asked for his medicine chest and chose a dose. Then, Susi remembered, he told him all was well and he could go. Before dawn Majwara saw him kneeling by the bed and thought he was praying. Later, frightened that he hadn’t moved, he woke the others. Matthew Wellington laid his hands on Livingstone’s cheeks. They were cold.

Hold that picture carefully: it is loved testimony, not a recording. Even the date is uncertain; his grave says 1 May 1873, but the men carved 4 May. If he died kneeling, it was in a position he had taken thousands of times.

The men could have buried him there and gone home. Instead they met, chose Susi and Chuma as leaders, and decided to carry his body and his papers to the coast, so his people could bury him and his work wouldn’t be lost. Nobody ordered them. They chose it.

Farijala, who had once watched a doctor work, and Carus Farrar removed his heart, and they buried it under a mpundu tree. Jacob Wainwright is said to have read the burial service, and he carved Livingstone’s name and the date in the tree. They dried the body in the sun, wrapped it in bark and sailcloth, and set off.

It was about a thousand miles. Several of them died on the way. When villages refused to let a corpse pass, they disguised the body as a bale of goods. When a British officer they met advised them to bury it inland, they refused. In February 1874, nine months after his death, they reached the coast.

Then most of them were paid off and sent home. Only Jacob went to England. He walked among the pallbearers at Westminster Abbey, beside Stanley. The grave says, “Brought by faithful hands over land and sea.” The hands over land were theirs. Later Susi and Chuma came to England and told the story that fills his last journals. Susi was baptised in 1886 and took the name David.

A month after he died, on 5 June 1873, the Sultan of Zanzibar signed a treaty closing the great slave market. A church now stands where people were sold. Missions in Malawi and Zambia grew into large churches, built mostly by African evangelists, as Livingstone had once said they would be. But his name was also used to justify British colonial rule, with its seized land and forced labour, which he would have hated. Africans have every right to make up their own minds about him.

He baptised one known convert. He was brave and stubborn, honest and unfair, devoted and costly to those who loved him. He gave himself to Christ at twenty and again at sixty. Like a grain of wheat, he bore most of his fruit after he died, through people like Sechele, Susi and Chuma.

One thing to do this week: find out the name of one person who quietly serves in your church or school without credit. Thank them by name, and ask God to help you be faithful even when no one is watching.

study_questions.answer: It comes from the men’s later memories, recorded by Waller, and can’t be checked. Even the date of his death is uncertain.

study_questions.question: How did his life bear fruit after his death?
study_questions.answer: The Zanzibar slave market closed, and missions in the lands he explored grew into large African-led churches. Sechele, Susi and Chuma carried the faith on.
